HOW TO USE THIS DECK

Prerequisites: C functions, if statements, pointers and compilation. You will write testable requirements, define module
contracts, review code and explain test levels.
KEY TAKEAWAY Concepts stick when you draw them and then use them — not when you read them once.
3
Learn it in three passes, not one
WHAT IS SOFTWARE ENGINEERING
The definition
Applying engineering discipline so
software is correct, maintainable
and delivered predictably.
Programming
Making one program work today.
Success is judged by one
question: does it run on my
machine?
Engineering
Making a system work for years,
under change, in many hands.
Success is judged by evidence.
A defined process
Requirements, design, review,
test and release are named
activities with entry and exit
criteria.
Real constraints
Cost, schedule, memory, timing,
power, safety and standards
shape every technical decision.
Deliberate trade-offs
There is no 'best' design — only
the one that best fits the
constraints you were given.
KEY TAKEAWAY Programming produces code; software engineering produces a system other people can trust, verify and change.
4
Engineering is programming plus process, constraints and
proof
WHY IT IS REQUIRED AND HOW IT HELPS
Software outlives its author
A C project may pass to another
student team. Clear modules and
build instructions help them
continue.
Change is the normal state
A changed pass mark can affect
code and tests. Written rules
make the impact easier to
identify.
Defects get expensive fast
A wrong result found before
submission is easier to repair
than one copied into many
reports.
Many hands, one system
Interfaces, ownership and
standards let a dozen people
build something coherent in
parallel.
Predictable delivery
Estimates, tracking and a
definition of done replace
guesswork with a plan you can
commit to.
Evidence when it matters
Requirements, review records
and test results let another
person check your work.
KEY TAKEAWAY You adopt engineering practice not to go slower, but to still be going fast in month six.
5
Discipline pays back in defects avoided, time saved and
change made safe
WHY ENGINEERING PRACTICE EXISTS
Solo hobby project Medium-scale team system
• One head holds the whole design • Design must be visible to others
• Style is whatever you prefer • Style is an agreed team contract
• 'It works on my laptop' is enough • It must work on everyone's build
• Bugs cost you an evening • Bugs cost the whole team days
• Memory is the documentation • Written artefacts are the memory
KEY TAKEAWAY Every practice in this module exists to replace one person's memory with shared, checkable artefacts.
6
Writing code alone is not software engineering
SCALE AND ITS CONSEQUENCES
5–30 illustrative team size
across 2–4 teams 50k–500k illustrative C codebase
size
n(n-1)/2 communication paths
in a team of n rework when teams discover
mismatched
assumptions
A team of 4 has 6 communication paths; a team of 12 has 66. You cannot fix that by talking more — you fix it with
interfaces, ownership and written agreements that let people work without asking.
KEY TAKEAWAY Beyond a handful of people, the bottleneck shifts from writing code to agreeing about code.
7
Medium-scale means coordination becomes the hard part
ILLUSTRATIVE LAB PROJECT
Running project: a student-marks program in C
8
One integer mark in. One clear result out. No hardware or external test
framework.
Agreed behaviour
Valid marks: 0 to 100 inclusive.
Pass: 40 to 100. Fail: 0 to 39.
Invalid mark or NULL output: return an error and
leave output unchanged.
These rules are invented for this lab.
Files and responsibilities
main.c: console interaction
marks.h: public contract
marks.c: classification rules
test_marks.c: automated checks
KEY TAKEAWAY The same requirement, function and tests recur throughout the module.
SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT LIFE CYCLE
Requirements
What must it do?
Design
How is it structured?
Implementation
Write the code
Testing
Prove it behaves
Release
Ship & deploy
Maintenance
Fix & evolve
feedback: every phase can send work back to an earlier one — that is normal, not failure
Waterfall
Work moves through planned
phases. Feedback may arrive late if
testing waits until implementation
ends.
Iterative / Agile
Short cycles deliver a working
increment, followed by feedback
and revision.
V-Model
Pair each design level with the tests
that check it. Plan both together.
KEY TAKEAWAY The phases never disappear — models only change how often you go round the loop.
9
The SDLC is one loop of six repeating activities
THE V-MODEL
Requirements
classify marks from 0 to 100
Architecture
main.c uses marks.h
Detailed design
range check and pass threshold
Unit test
does 40 produce pass = 1?
Integration / system
API calls / complete console run
Acceptance test
does it meet the lab brief?
Implementation in marks.c
KEY TAKEAWAY Write the test plan for a level at the same time as the design for that level — not months later.
10
Every level of design is answered by a level of testing
REQUIREMENT UNDERSTANDING
1Unambiguous
One reading only. No 'fast', 'user-friendly', 'as needed'.
2Testable
You can name the test that proves it passes or fails.
3Traceable
It has an ID and links to design, code and tests.
4Feasible & bounded
Achievable with the chosen C tools and project
scope.
✗ Weak
"The program shall process marks correctly."
Try this: specify the valid range, pass boundary and
invalid-input behaviour.
Strong (REQ-M1)
For an integer mark from 0 to 100, mark_classify shall
return MARK_OK and set *passed to 1 for marks >= 40,
otherwise 0.
KEY TAKEAWAY Rewrite every vague requirement into a number, a condition and an observable result before coding.
11
A requirement you cannot test is only a wish
ASKING BETTER QUESTIONS
Who? Who uses this, and what do they do immediately before and after?
What if not? What happens on invalid input, a NULL pointer or a file error?
How many / how fast? Numbers: valid input range, record count, memory and runtime limits.
Who else is affected? Which other modules, teams or products see this change?
How will we know? Which input and expected result demonstrate success?
KEY TAKEAWAY Requirements are rarely written down wrong — they are usually not written down at all. Ask, then record.
12
Five questions that expose most hidden requirements
NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS
Runtime target
Lab example: process 1,000 records within 1 s on the
named lab PC.
Memory limit
Lab example: use at most 100 int elements for a stored
batch.
Portability
Use standard C11 features. Avoid operating-system-specific
calls.
Robustness
Invalid input must not crash the program or change valid
stored data.
Usability
State the allowed mark range in every invalid-input
message.
Maintainability
Keep console input/output separate from mark
classification.
Verification method
Record the input, environment, method and expected limit.
Try this: write one measurable quality constraint for your C
project.
KEY TAKEAWAY These are illustrative lab constraints. Agree each target and its verification method before coding.

Why traceability pays for itself
•Change impact: when REQ-M1 changes, identify the affected function and tests.
•Coverage: a missing link shows where test evidence still needs checking.
•Review: connect each requirement to a test result and the version tested.
•Onboarding: read backwards from code to the intended behaviour.
KEY TAKEAWAY Traceability is not paperwork — it is the map you need on the day something breaks.

BASIC DESIGN THINKING
Separation of concerns
Each module has one reason to
exist — and one reason to
change.
Information hiding
Hide the data and the how;
publish only the what.
Low coupling
Modules depend on few others,
through narrow interfaces.
High cohesion
Everything inside a module
belongs to the same job.
Layering
main.c calls the public marks.h
interface. marks.c does not call
main.c.
Design for change
Isolate the rules likely to change,
such as the pass threshold or
output format.
KEY TAKEAWAY Ask of every module: what does it hide? If it hides nothing, it is not a module — it is a folder.
16
Good design is a decision about where to put the boundaries
LAYERED ARCHITECTURE
Console application main.c coordinates input, classification and
output
Public interface marks.h declares status values and
mark_classify()
Module implementation marks.c checks the range and computes
pass/fail
Private helper functions static helpers remain inside marks.c when
needed
Basic C operations integer comparisons, logical operators and
assignment
uses
Why it helps
•Test marks.c without
keyboard input.
•Change console
messages without
changing
classification.
•Assign a reviewer to
each module.
KEY TAKEAWAY Keep the marks module independent of console input/output and avoid circular dependencies.
17
A C program separates input/output from calculation
INTERFACE THINKING IN C
marks.h: the public contract
#ifndef MARKS_H
#define MARKS_H
typedef enum { MARK_OK, MARK_INVALID }
mark_status_t;
/* mark: 0..100; passed: writable int.
OK: sets 1 if mark >= 40, else 0.
INVALID: bad mark or NULL pointer.
On INVALID, leaves output unchanged. */
mark_status_t mark_classify(int mark,
int *passed);
#endif
A contract answers five questions
1Purpose — what one job does this call do?
2Parameters — valid ranges, ownership of pointers
3Return — every status value and its meaning
4Errors — what the caller must handle
5Constraints: no input/output, no global state, no
allocation.
KEY TAKEAWAY Keep headers small and stable: everything not in the header is free to change tomorrow.
18
The header file is the contract; the .c file is nobody's business
BEFORE AND AFTER: C HEADER
A small interface makes the contract explicit
19
Weak interface
extern int result;
void check(int x);
What does x mean?
What happens on invalid input?
Who may change result?
Improved interface
mark_status_t mark_classify(
int mark, int *passed);
Name the input and its range.
Return MARK_OK or MARK_INVALID.
Write through a caller-owned pointer.
Keep error behaviour in the header.
KEY TAKEAWAY A caller can use the function without reading marks.c.
INTERFACE HYGIENE
Expose functions, not globals
extern int g_state; is a hole in your module wall.
static by default
Give private file-scope functions and objects static linkage.
One header, one concern
Do not create util.h that everyone includes.
Include guards
Use #ifndef / #define / #endif around each header.
Return status, don't hide failure
void functions that can fail are landmines.
Choose suitable types
int is sufficient for marks 0..100 and the values 0 or 1.
Document units and ownership
Marks are whole numbers. The caller owns the output int.
Try this: move one private declaration from your header into
its .c file.
KEY TAKEAWAY A narrow interface is a promise you can keep; a wide one is a promise you will break.
20
Seven habits that keep a C interface from rotting
MODULE OWNERSHIP
Knows the design
Can explain why the
module is built this way.
Guards the interface
Approves every change to
the public header.
Keeps quality
Tests, docs, static-
analysis warnings,
technical debt list.
Reviews & mentors
Reviews changes from
others and teaches the
area.
Ownership means
Accountability for the module's health, and a named
person to ask. Anyone may propose a change.
Ownership does NOT mean
A private kingdom, a bus factor of one, or the right to
block work without a technical reason.
KEY TAKEAWAY Every module needs a name next to it — and a second person who could take over next week.
21
An owner is a steward, not a gatekeeper
CODE REVIEW
1
Author prepares
small change, self-
reviewed, builds &
tests pass
2
Reviewer reads
intent first, then
correctness, then style
3
Comments
specific, kind, with a
reason
4
Author responds
fix or explain — every
comment answered
5
Approve & merge
re-run tests, then
merge
What to look for
•Does it match the requirement and the design?
•Check NULL, valid ranges and boundary
comparisons.
•Check initialization and output changes on errors.
•Are tests convincing? Is console I/O separate?
Review etiquette
•Review the code, never the person.
•Keep each change small enough to understand fully.
•Say why: "40 must pass, so use >= rather than >."
•Use a shared format so reviewers focus on logic.
KEY TAKEAWAY Reviews spread knowledge as much as they catch bugs — that is why everyone reviews,
not just seniors.
22
Review defends the design, not your ego

Code-review exercise: find three contract violations
23
Proposed marks.c change
#include "marks.h"
mark_status_t mark_classify(int mark,
int *passed)
{
*passed = (mark > 40);
return MARK_OK;
}
Review prompts
1. What happens at 40?
2. What happens at -1 or 101?
3. What happens with NULL?
Write a comment that names the
issue, consequence and fix.
KEY TAKEAWAY Review against marks.h. The answer appendix gives a corrected implementation.
BEYOND CODE REVIEW
Requirement review Before design Ambiguity, missing error cases, untestable wording
Design / architecture review Before coding Wrong boundaries, circular dependencies, missed constraints
Code review Per change Logic, edge cases, readability, test quality
Test review With the tests Weak assertions, untested branches, missing negative tests
Review early to catch mistakes before they spread into dependent code and tests. The cost of rework depends on the
project.
24
Four review types, each catching a different class of defect
TESTING LEVELS
Unit Does this function do what its contract says?
test_marks.c calls mark_classify() using assert checks
Integration Do modules agree at their interfaces?
main.c and marks.c agree on status and output values
System Does the whole product meet the requirements?
complete console run: input, classification and displayed result
Acceptance Does it meet the agreed lab brief?
tutor checks agreed example inputs and
results
Test effort: many fast unit tests at the widest band, fewer integration tests, and few slow system and acceptance
tests.
25
Each level answers a different question — none replaces
another
DESIGNING GOOD TESTS
1
Equivalence classes
Group inputs that behave alike; test one from each
group.
2
Boundary values
For marks: -1, 0, 39, 40, 100 and 101.
3
Negative tests
NULL output pointer, out-of-range mark, invalid
text input.
4
State coverage
For a menu extension: input, error, retry and exit
paths.
5
Stubs & mocks
Use a controlled replacement for file or keyboard
input.
6
Coverage as a hint
Line/branch coverage finds untested code — it
never proves correctness.
KEY TAKEAWAY Deliberately change >= to > and check that the test for mark 40 fails.
26
Test the boundaries, the errors and the ugly inputs
ARRANGE, ACT, ASSERT
A complete C unit test for the pass boundary
27
#include <assert.h>
#include "marks.h"
int main(void)
{
int passed = -1; /* arrange */
mark_status_t status;
status = mark_classify(40, &passed);
assert(status == MARK_OK);
assert(passed == 1); /* assert */
return 0;
}
Prove the test detects a fault
Correct code uses >= 40.
Change it to > 40, rebuild and run.
The second assertion must fail.
Restore >= and rerun. Do not define
NDEBUG for this test.
gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic marks.c test_marks.c -o test_marks
Run ./test_marks (Windows: test_marks.exe). Success exits normally with no output.
QUALITY ASSURANCE CONCEPTS
Quality Assurance — preventive
Team coding rules, compiler warnings, automated
builds, definition of done and process checks. Aim:
prevent defects.
Quality Control — detective
Reviews, test execution, defect tracking, release
verification. Aim: find defects that were created
anyway.
Static analysis
compiler warnings and
tools such as cppcheck
Continuous
integration
every push: build, unit
test, analyse, report
Defect management
log, triage, root-cause,
verify the fix
Metrics
escaped defects,
coverage, build health,
review latency
KEY TAKEAWAY Quality is a property of the process; you cannot test it into a product at the end.
28
QA builds the process; testing measures the product
CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT
Version control everything
Source, headers, build commands and test data, not just .c
files.
Branching model
Short-lived feature branches off main; merge only green
builds.
Pin the toolchain
Compiler version and flags are part of the product, not the
laptop.
Reproducible builds
Record all build inputs and the environment. Compare
rebuilt outputs.
Release baselines and tags
Tag every release; record requirement, test and binary
versions together.
Change control
Every change traces to an issue ID; no silent commits to a
released branch.
Archive the artifacts
Store the executable, compiler version and build/test logs.
Try this: rebuild a tagged version with the recorded compiler
and commands.
KEY TAKEAWAY Configuration management is what turns a pile of commits into a product you can ship, audit and fix.
29
If you cannot rebuild last year's release, you do not own it
COLLABORATION PRACTICES
1Version control
discipline
Short-lived branches, small
commits, messages that say why.
2Definition of done
Coded + reviewed + unit tested +
documented + CI green.
3Daily sync, 15 minutes
Done / next / blocked. Problems go
to a follow-up, not the standup.
4Written decisions
A one-page design note beats a
remembered corridor conversation.
5Issue tracker as truth
If it is not a ticket, it will not happen.
6Retrospectives
Improve the process every iteration;
fix causes, not people.
KEY TAKEAWAY Agree the rules once, write them down, and stop re-deciding them in every conversation.
30
Shared rules beat constant coordination
PUTTING IT TOGETHER: ILLUSTRATIVE SEQUENCE
Mon Agree REQ-M1 and error cases. Write expected results for the boundary values.
Tue Declare mark_classify() in marks.h. Ask two peers to review the contract.
Wed Write test_marks.c, then implement marks.c until the tests pass.
Thu Resolve review comments. Build and run tests before merging.
Fri Connect main.c to marks.c. Test console input/output against the lab brief.
Illustrative sequence, not a five-day estimate. Each step produces evidence another person can check.

ANSWER APPENDIX
Review answer: validate before writing the result
34
#include <stddef.h>
#include "marks.h"
mark_status_t mark_classify(int mark,
int *passed)
{
if (passed == NULL ||
mark < 0 || mark > 100)
return MARK_INVALID;
*passed = (mark >= 40);
return MARK_OK;
}
Model review comment
“At mark 40, > returns fail, but REQ-
M1 requires pass. Use >=.
Check the pointer and range before
writing. Invalid input must return
MARK_INVALID without changing
output.”
KEY TAKEAWAY All seven contract cases belong in the tests, including unchanged output on error.

INTRODUCTORY C ENGINEERING LAB
An end-to-end introductory
software engineering example in C
37
One small program, a complete introductory workflow
The program classifies marks as PASS, FAIL or INVALID.
The engineering work explains how a team agrees on rules, checks the C code
and hands over a reproducible version.
16 steps: requirements, team plan, Git setup, design, C code, tests, automation, review,
acceptance, evidence, quality, release and maintenance.
Teaching scope: an introductory lifecycle. Large-system architecture, production operations, security
engineering and regulation need further study.

The problem and its acceptance criteria
38
Goal: classify a small list of student marks with a reusable, testable C function.
Requirement

Pass at 40 or above.

-

Output remains unchanged.

Return MARK_INVALID without

Scope: use a fixed array, not keyboard input. No database, files or hardware are required.

The file structure and public contract

Create marks.h
#ifndef MARKS_H
#define MARKS_H
typedef enum { MARK_OK, MARK_INVALID }
mark_status_t;
/* Valid mark: 0..100. Caller owns *passed.
OK: write 1 for >=40, otherwise 0.
INVALID: bad mark or NULL pointer.
Leave output unchanged on INVALID. */
mark_status_t mark_classify(int mark,
int *passed);
#endif

The implementation follows the contract
42
Create marks.c
#include <stddef.h>
#include "marks.h"
mark_status_t mark_classify(int mark,
int *passed)
{
if (passed == NULL ||
mark < 0 || mark > 100) {
return MARK_INVALID;
}
*passed = (mark >= 40);
return MARK_OK;
}
Algorithm, in order
1. Check the output pointer.
2. Check the mark range.
3. If either check fails, return before
writing anything.
4. Otherwise write 0 or 1 and return
MARK_OK.
Dry run for 40: pointer valid, range valid, 40 >= 40 is true, so write 1.

Unit tests for valid marks
43
Create test_marks.c, part 1 of 2
#include <assert.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include "marks.h"
static void expect_valid(int mark,
int expected)
{
int passed = -1;
mark_status_t s;
s = mark_classify(mark, &passed);
assert(s == MARK_OK);
assert(passed == expected);
}
How this helper works
Arrange: set a sentinel (-1).
Act: call the real function.
Assert: check both status and
output.
The next slide calls this helper for 0,
39, 40 and 100.
Keep assertions enabled. Do not compile the test with -DNDEBUG.

Error-path tests and the test runner
44
Append to test_marks.c, part 2 of 2
static void expect_invalid(int mark)
{int passed = -1;
mark_status_t s;
s = mark_classify(mark, &passed);
assert(s == MARK_INVALID);
assert(passed == -1);
}
int main(void)
{expect_valid(0, 0);
expect_valid(39, 0);
expect_valid(40, 1);
expect_valid(100, 1);
expect_invalid(-1);
expect_invalid(101);
mark_status_t s = mark_classify(40, NULL);
assert(s == MARK_INVALID);
puts("All 7 cases passed");
return 0;
}
What these checks protect
Invalid marks must leave the
sentinel unchanged.
The NULL case must return an
error safely.
Only after all seven cases finish
does the program print its success
message.
Save parts 1 and 2 together in one
test_marks.c.

Create main.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include "marks.h"
int main(void)
{int marks[] = {-1, 0, 39, 40, 100, 101};
size_t count = sizeof marks / sizeof marks[0];
for (size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
int passed = -1;
mark_status_t s;
s = mark_classify(marks[i], &passed);
if (s == MARK_INVALID)
printf("%d: INVALID\n", marks[i]);
elseprintf("%d: %s\n", marks[i],
passed ? "PASS" : "FAIL");
}
return 0;
}
Follow one iteration
For mark 40:
1. Set passed to -1.
2. Call the module.
3. Status is MARK_OK.
4. Print 40: PASS.

Create check.sh for a POSIX shell, such as Linux, macOS or WSL.
#!/bin/sh
set -eu
CC=${CC:-gcc}
CFLAGS="-std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Werror"
mkdir -p build
$CC $CFLAGS marks.c test_marks.c -o build/test_marks
$CC $CFLAGS marks.c main.c -o build/marks_demo
./build/test_marks
./build/marks_demo > build/actual.txt
diff -u expected.txt build/actual.txt
echo "Build, unit and system checks passed"
expected.txt
-1: INVALID
0: FAIL
39: FAIL
40: PASS
100: PASS
101: INVALID
